title: Rotating the Box
statement:
`boxGrid` is an `m x n` side view of a box in which every cell holds a stone `'#'`, a fixed obstacle `'*'`, or nothing `'.'`.

Turn the box a quarter turn clockwise. After the turn, each stone drops straight down until the cell below it is an obstacle, another stone, or the floor of the box. Obstacles never move, and stones never shift sideways. Return the resulting `n x m` grid.

The input is already at rest under its own gravity: below every stone of `boxGrid` there is an obstacle, a stone, or the bottom edge of the box.
constraints: Before the turn, every stone sits on an obstacle, a stone or the bottom row
notes:
## Intuition

After a clockwise quarter turn, each original row becomes a column of the new grid, and "down" in the new grid means "to the right" in the original row. So the whole job is: inside every row, slide stones to the right until they hit an obstacle, another stone, or the row's end, then write the row out as a column. A brute force can build the turned grid and keep swapping any stone with an empty cell below it until nothing moves, but that can take many passes.

## Approach

1. Create `result` with `n` rows and `m` columns, filled with `'.'`.
2. For row `i`, its cells land in column `col = m - 1 - i`, and cell `j` lands in `result[j][col]`.
3. Scan the row from right to left with a second pointer `empty`: the lowest free spot a stone can fall to, starting at `n - 1`.
4. An obstacle stays at `j` and resets `empty` to `j - 1`, because nothing can fall past it.
5. A stone is written at `empty`, and `empty` moves one step left (up, after the turn).
6. Empty cells are skipped; they are already `'.'` in `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

`boxGrid = [["#",".","#"]]`, so `m = 1`, `n = 3` and `col = 0`. `empty` starts at `2`. At `j = 2` a stone goes to `result[2][0]` and `empty` becomes `1`. `j = 1` is empty. At `j = 0` the stone goes to `result[1][0]` and `empty` becomes `0`. The answer is `[["."],["#"],["#"]]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m · n): every cell is read once and written at most once.
- Space: O(m · n) for the returned grid; the scan itself uses O(1).

## Pitfalls

- The rotation is clockwise: row `i` becomes column `m - 1 - i`, not column `i`.
- Stones fall toward the end of each original row, so scan right to left; scanning left to right misplaces stacks.
- After an obstacle, `empty` must restart just before it, even if earlier spots were still free.
- The answer is `n x m`, not `m x n`; build it with the swapped sizes.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `m`, `n` | rows and columns of `boxGrid` |
| `result` | the turned grid, `n` rows by `m` columns |
| `i`, `j` | current row and cell in `boxGrid` |
| `col` | column of `result` that row `i` becomes |
| `empty` | lowest free row in `col` where the next stone lands |
| `cell` | the character at `boxGrid[i][j]` |

narration.4: Start the turned grid as all empty: n rows by m columns.
narration.6: Handle one original row at a time; it becomes a single column after the turn.
narration.7: Clockwise turning sends row i to column m - 1 - i.
narration.8: The first stone of this row can fall all the way to the bottom, row n - 1.
narration.9: Scan from the bottom of the new column, which is the right end of the row.
narration.12: ...so copy it to the same height in the new column.
narration.13: Nothing can fall past it, so the next free spot is just above it.
narration.14: A stone drops as far as it can.
narration.15: Place it at the lowest free spot.
narration.16: That spot is taken now; the next stone stacks one above it.
narration.20: Every row has been dropped into its column; return the turned grid.
